examples.title: Unpaired two-sample t test
examples.prompt: Subjects over 65 with cognitive decline were split into a control group (\(n_1 = 22\), \(\bar x_1 = 49\), \(s_1 = 8.4\)) and a treatment group of diet, exercise and brain training (\(n_2 = 27\), \(\bar x_2 = 57\), \(s_2 = 9.5\)). Is there a difference in cognitive scores between the two populations?

steps.say: The test is the unpaired two-sample t test, because the control group and the treatment group are made of different subjects.
The null hypothesis is that there is no difference in cognitive scores between the control group and the treatment group.
These are the general equations, written before any numbers go in.
Weight each squared SD by its group size minus 1 and divide by the total degrees of freedom. This gives one shared variance.
The standard error of the difference is 2.5921, so the means are about 3.1 standard errors apart.
Both groups lose one degree of freedom for their own mean.
Row 47 is not printed, so the cutoff sits between rows 46 and 48 in the 0.05 column. The size of t is larger, so reject at 0.05.
The size of t also beats the 0.01 cutoff. There is a difference in cognitive scores between the control group and the treatment group, with P less than 0.01.

examples.title: One-sample t test
examples.prompt: The average LDL of USC faculty and staff is 115 mg/dL. A random sample of 16 USC undergraduates had mean LDL 103 mg/dL with SD 16 mg/dL. Is there a significant difference in LDL between USC undergraduates and the faculty and staff value?

steps.say: The test is the one-sample t test. The null hypothesis is that mean LDL in USC undergraduates is not different from the faculty and staff value of 115 mg/dL.
These are the general equations, written before any numbers go in.
The standard error is 4 mg/dL, so the sample mean sits 3 standard errors below 115.
One mean was estimated from the 16 students, so there are 15 degrees of freedom. Row 15 is printed in the two-tailed t table.
The size of t passes both cutoffs, so reject the null hypothesis. Mean LDL in USC undergraduates differs from the faculty and staff value of 115 mg/dL, with P less than 0.01.
